part.text:
The client (via Jorge, the partner) is pushing back: the other defendant's lawyer is "guaranteeing" that it's doubled under Article 229 of the CPC (Brazilian Code of Civil Procedure). The user is asking me: are we really sure it's not doubled? "If we underestimate it, we'll miss the deadline."

Wait — actually, there's an interesting point here: "Se errarmos pra menos, perdemos o prazo" — if we err by assuming the shorter side, we lose the deadline. In practice, if we assume no doubling (15 days), we diarize the earlier deadline (12/15/2026) — that's the safe direction. If it actually turned out to be doubled, then filing early is no problem — early filing is never a problem. The risk direction: assuming double when it's actually single means missing the deadline. The partner's concern seems confused — but I should address it politely: planning for the shorter (single) deadline is conservative and safe.

Now the legal issue: Article 229, main clause (caput) vs. paragraph 2 (§2º). The library's cpc_prazos.md explicitly includes Article 229, §2º: "The provisions of the caput shall not apply to proceedings conducted in electronic form (autos eletrônicos)." The case is electronic (e-SAJ, "electronic proceedings (processo eletrônico)" written on both summons documents). So within the closed library, doubling is clearly excluded. The other lawyer's assertion of "Article 229 of the CPC" ignores paragraph 2.

I can also mention the subsidiary argument from paragraph 1 (§1º): even if doubling applied, if there are only 2 defendants and only one files a defense, the doubling ends — but this is moot.

Also a practical risk analysis:
- Diarize the single deadline (12/15): if the doubling theory turns out to be correct later, filing on 12/15 is still valid (early filing within the doubled period). Filing early is never out of time. Therefore the "errar pra menos (erring on the lower side)" strategy is risk-free on the answer.
- For the appeal: diarizing 2027-02-03 (single) — early filing is also fine.
- The dangerous direction is trusting the doubling (answer on 1/19/2027+… no wait, doubled would be 30 business days; answer expires around January + recess period) — if paragraph 2 applies, the appeal filed on 2/28/2027 is… no let me calculate: doubled appeal = 30 business days → expires around February 2027, and if the deadline was actually single (2/3/2027), that's too late → out of time, losing the right.

So the safe path is exactly what we did. I should be confident and cite the library precisely: the very provision the other lawyer cites — Article 229 — contains paragraph 2, which excludes electronic case files (autos eletrônicos), and both summons documents state "PROCESSO ELETRÔNICO (e-SAJ)."

Is there any room for doubt? In real-world Brazilian law, the STJ (Superior Court of Justice) interpreted Article 229, §2º restrictively (the famous thesis: doubling applies to the Public Defender's Office (Defensoria) and the Treasury (Fazenda) even in electronic proceedings — actually that's a different issue: CPC/2015 Article 229, §2º excludes litisconsortes with different attorneys in electronic proceedings; the STJ's 1st Panel had discussed this… there's real-world case law: the STJ held that Article 229, §2º applies and there is no doubling for litisconsortes with different attorneys in electronic proceedings. The Doubling statute for the Public Defender's Office (LC 80/94, Law 13.357… etc.) applies regardless of whether proceedings are electronic. But the Public Defender's Office/Fazenda is not involved in this case.) The library is closed and I can't verify anything outside the library — so I should state: I cannot verify case law from outside the library; based on the library alone, the text is explicit. Real-world nuance: some scholars/courts once discussed whether "different offices" still deserve doubling in electronic proceedings, but the statutory text is clear. Also worth noting: since 2016, DJe/e-SAJ means simultaneous intimation — the rationale for doubling (staggered publication dates across different attorneys/ DJE cadernos) has vanished, which is why §2º exists. That rationale can only be mentioned as reasoning if labeled as unverified outside the library… no, actually the rationale discussion is just commentary; I can briefly explain it as a general observation and label it as unverified since it's not in the library. Better: stick to the text, and mention that I checked the library for any provisions supporting doubling — and there are none.

The deliverables should also be updated: add a short section to memoria.md (or an addendum) answering this specific pushback — because the deliverables are the work product. The client's reply came in as a turn; per the contract, client questions go to QUESTIONS.md and I respond on the next turn. Now the client asked me a question. I should respond in chat and record the answer in the deliverables (e.g., add an "Annex — On the alleged deadline doubling (ANEXO — Sobre a alegada prazo em dobro)" section to memoria.md, update STATUS.md if needed). That's good practice: the deliverables should carry the answer.

A concrete risk analysis with dates:
- If single (correct, per §2º): answer expires 12/15/2026; appeal expires 2/3/2027.
- If doubled (the other lawyer's theory): answer is 30 business days from 11/24/2026 → let me calculate: days 16–30: business days from 12/16 onward, skipping the recess period 12/20–1/20: 12/16(16), 12/17(17), 12/18(18), then resuming 1/21(19), 1/22(20), 1/25(21), 1/26(22), 1/27(23), 1/28(24), 1/29(25), 2/1(26), 2/2(27), 2/3(28), 2/4(29), 2/5(30) → 2/5/2027. Appeal doubled: 30 business days from 12/14: days 1–5 (12/14–18), 6–15 resume as before ending 2/3/2027 (day 15), then days 16–30: 2/4(16), 2/5(17), 2/8? — 2/8–2/9/2027 is Carnival (listed as holidays on the calendar) → skip, 2/10 (Wed, day 18)… wait, 2027-02-10 is a Wednesday. Checking day of week: 2/1/2027 Monday, 2/3 Wednesday, 2/4 Thursday, 2/5 Friday, 2/8 Monday (listed as Carnival on calendar), 2/9 Tuesday (Carnaval), 2/10 Wednesday, 2/11 Thursday, 2/12 Friday, 2/15 Monday, 2/16 Tuesday, 2/17 Wednesday, 2/18 Thursday, 2/19 Friday, 2/22 Monday, 2/23 Tuesday, 2/24 Wednesday, 2/25 Thursday, 2/26 Friday, 2/27 Saturday… days: 16=2/4 Thu, 17=2/5 Fri, 18=2/10 Wed, 19=2/11 Thu, 20=2/12 Fri, 21=2/15 Mon, 22=2/16 Tue, 23=2/17 Wed, 24=2/18 Thu, 25=2/19 Fri, 26=2/22 Mon, 27=2/23 Tue, 28=2/24 Wed, 29=2/25 Thu, 30=2/26 Fri → doubled appeal expires 2/26/2027 (before Carnival… note there's no Ash Wednesday on the 2027 calendar; also, 2/8–9 Carnival is treated as non-business days). I can run this through Python.

The asymmetry of risk: planning for the shorter deadline = filing early = always safe (within time under either theory). Planning for double when it's actually single = out of time. So the "errar pra menos" concern is backwards: erring downward is precisely the safe direction. What's dangerous is erring upward (trusting the doubling).

But also note: there's no need to hedge legally — §2º is clear on its face in the library. And even under a belt-and-suspenders view, the practical recommendation doesn't change: diarize 12/15/2026 and 2/3/2027; if there's excess capacity, also file earlier.

Another check: the possibility that the other lawyer is relying on some old rule or a different basis? Article 229 of CPC/2015 is exactly what we have. Also, "different offices" is a prerequisite, and §2º eliminates it in autos eletrônicos. Both intimation documents literally state "PROCESSO ELETRÔNICO (e-SAJ)" — the factual predicate for §2º is met on the face of the records.

Furthermore, §1º gives an independent safety note: even if doubling existed, it would end once only one defendant files a defense.

What I should do:
1. Run a quick Python calculation for the doubled hypothetical dates (to show the other lawyer's world's expiry dates and where the risk would fall).
2. Add an annex to memoria.md (ANEXO) with the response: textual citation of §2º, facts (e-SAJ on both PDFs), risk asymmetry, dates for both scenarios, recommendation: diarize the single dates.
3. Update open items in STATUS.md if needed — add a line that the doubling question was answered with an annex. Keep it COMPLETE WITH OPEN ITEMS.
4. Reply concisely to Jorge in chat.

I should also mention the honest caveat: since the library is closed, I cannot verify case law; if in the real world the other lawyer had case law saying the doubling survives in electronic proceedings, it would not be in the library — but the statutory text they themselves cite says the opposite, and the safe diarization strategy protects us regardless.

Let me calculate the hypothetical doubled dates in Python.

from datetime import date, timedelta
holidays = {date(2026,11,20),date(2026,12,8),date(2026,12,24),date(2026,12,25),date(2026,12,31),
            date(2027,1,1),date(2027,2,8),date(2027,2,9)}
susp = (date(2026,12,20), date(2027,1,20))
def workable(d): return d.weekday()<5 and d not in holidays and not (susp[0]<=d<=susp[1])
def count(start,n):
    d,day=start,0
    while day<n:
        if workable(d): day+=1; day_data=d
        d+=timedelta(1)
    return day_data
WD={0:'seg',1:'ter',2:'qua',3:'qui',4:'sex',5:'sab',6:'dom'}

print("  contestacao  : venc", count(date(2026,11,24),30), WD[count(date(2026,11,24),30).weekday()])
print("  apelacao     : venc", count(date(2026,12,14),30), WD[count(date(2026,12,14),30).weekday()])
print("CONTAGEM CORRETA (simplo, art.229 §2o):")
print("  contestacao  : venc", count(date(2026,11,24),15))
print("  apelacao     : venc", count(date(2026,12,14),15))
EOF

O pressuposto fático do §2º está **na capa das duas intimações**: "PROCESSO ELETRÔNICO (e-SAJ)" (ambos os PDFs em `documents/`). A dobra do *caput* exige litisconsortes com procuradores de escritórios distintos — o requisito existe (fls. 61/70) — mas a natureza eletrônica dos autos **afasta a dobra**, independentemente da experiência de quem quer que afirme o contrário. A razão do §2º é que a dobra existe para compensar publicações escalonadas do DJe em cadernos diferentes por advogado; em autos eletrônicos a intimação é única para todos. *(Essa ratio é explicação doutrinária — não está na biblioteca; registro como não verificada. O que vale é o texto do §2º, esse sim no texto legal da biblioteca.)*

Nada na biblioteca sustenta a dobra neste caso: o único dispositivo sobre o tema (art. 229) contém a excludente do §2º. Argumento subsidiário, ainda que inútil: mesmo que houvesse dobra, ela **cessaria** se apenas uma das duas rés oferecesse defesa (art. 229, §1º).

**A direção do risco está invertida em relação à preocupação do sócio.** O erro perigoso é marcar o calendário pela dobra; o erro "para menos" é inofensivo, porque protocolar **antes** do prazo nunca é intempestivo:

| Cenário | Contestação | Apelação | Consequência se calendariarmos a DOBRA e a dobra não existir (que é o caso) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Correto — simplo (art. 229, §2º)** | 15/12/2026 | 03/02/2027 | — |
| Tese do outro advogado — dobro | 05/02/2027 | 26/02/2027 | contestação em 05/02/2027 = **revelia**; apelação em 26/02/2027 = **intempestiva, perde-se o recurso** (prazo verdadeiro: 03/02/2027) |

Ou seja: seguindo a "garantia" do advogado da outra ré, quem perde o prazo somos nós. **Recomendação: calendário nas datas em simplo — 15/12/2026 (contestação), 18/12/2026 (embargos, se quiser) e 03/02/2027 (apelação).** Protocolar antes disso é sempre seguro sob qualquer das duas teses.

*Ressalva de honestidade (biblioteca fechada):* não posso verificar jurisprudência fora da biblioteca; se o colega dispuser de decisão que salve a dobra em autos eletrônicos, ela não está em nosso acervo e não posso avaliá-la. Mas o texto do art. 229, §2º — que ele mesmo invoca o art. 229 — é expresso, e a recomendação acima não depende de resposta a essa dúvida: protege contra os dois cenários.
